name: Keratin straightening

lead: Keratin straightening, also called a Brazilian treatment, is a salon service that reduces frizz and wave and adds shine, leaving hair straighter and sleeker for roughly two to six months. The smoother look is visible straight after the session.

A keratin-containing product is applied to the hair and sealed in with a flat iron; the heat sets the coating onto the hair shaft and smooths the surface. It is described as less structurally permanent than relaxers. Published trial data are sparse, with one small registered study of unknown status.

paras: It is done in a salon over about two to four hours, and people typically repeat it as results fade over a few months. Many use sulfate-free aftercare to make it last.

Keratin treatments emit gases, skin and eye protection is required during application, and they are not recommended during pregnancy. Some products contain formaldehyde-releasing agents. The flat-iron heat can also damage hair.

angle.text: A keratin straightening treatment coats the hair with keratin and seals it with a flat iron, cutting frizz and wave and leaving hair straighter and shinier for roughly two to six months. The result is visible right after the session; controlled trial data are limited.

lead: Keratin straightening, also called a Brazilian treatment, is a salon smoothing procedure in which a keratin-containing product is applied to the hair and sealed in with a flat iron. Wikipedia describes it as reducing frizz and adding shine, lasting roughly two to six months, and taking about two to four hours.[1]

The category has attracted health discussion. Wikipedia notes that keratin treatments emit gases, that skin and eye protection is required, and that they are not recommended during pregnancy; some straightening products are described as containing formaldehyde-releasing agents.[1] Evidence for the treatments is limited: a small registered study of a keratin hair therapy exists, with unknown status.[2]

paras: A keratin layer is added to the hair and heat-sealed with a flat iron; unlike chemical relaxers, the effect is described as gradually washing out rather than permanently restructuring the hair.[1] Related ingredients are covered in the hydrolyzed keratin entry.

Wikipedia states that straightening products may contain formaldehyde-releasing agents and that fumes are emitted during use, with protective gear required and use not recommended in pregnancy.[1] Wikipedia also links to guidance from the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration on formaldehyde in hair-smoothing products.[1] Heat applied during straightening can damage hair, which Wikipedia says cannot be reversed except by cutting off the damaged hair.[1]

A registered study, NCT04489576 ("Evaluation of Safety and Efficacy of Keratin Hair Therapy"), planned 30 participants with hair damage, began in November 2020, and has unknown status with no posted results.[2]
